introduction-breaking-things-on-purpose.core: Chaos engineering injects controlled failures to verify that systems behave as expected under stress, revealing weaknesses before real incidents do. AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) runs managed experiments against AWS resources (EC2, ECS, EKS, RDS, network, APIs) with guardrails and stop conditions.

first_principles.problem: A team believes its service survives an AZ failure but has never tested it, until a real outage proves otherwise.
truths: Untested resilience is assumed, not known.
Real failures happen at bad times.

analogy.title: Fire drills
analogy.story: You practise evacuating when nothing is burning, so the real thing goes smoothly.
analogy.breaks: Fire drills don't cause fires; chaos experiments cause real (controlled) failures.

example.title: First experiment
flow: Hypothesis: losing 1 of 3 AZs keeps error rate < 1%
Finding: health check grace too long

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fixed before a real AZ failure.

check.a: A measurable statement of normal behaviour (e.g. error rate < 1%) that should hold during the experiment.

the-experiment-anatomy-templates-actions.core: An FIS experiment template defines actions (what fault: stop instances, inject CPU stress, throttle APIs, disrupt network, fail over RDS, terminate EKS pods), targets (which resources, by ARN, tags or filters, with selection mode like PERCENT(25)), stop conditions (CloudWatch alarms that halt the experiment) and an IAM role FIS uses.

first_principles.problem: An unbounded experiment hits all production instances because targets weren't scoped.

analogy.title: A controlled demolition plan
analogy.story: Which walls, how much charge, safety perimeter and an abort button.
analogy.breaks: Demolitions are irreversible; most FIS actions end automatically after their duration.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 30% of staging web instances stopped for 10 min; auto-abort on 5xx alarm.

check.q: What is the purpose of an FIS stop condition?
check.a: To automatically halt the experiment when a CloudWatch alarm indicates unacceptable impact.

deep-dive-the-ssm-integration-for-os-lev.core: For faults inside instances (CPU, memory and disk stress, process kill, network latency and packet loss), FIS runs Systems Manager documents (AWSFIS-Run-CPU-Stress, AWSFIS-Run-Network-Latency…) via the aws:ssm:send-command action on targeted instances. ECS and EKS actions inject similar faults into tasks and pods.

first_principles.problem: Stopping instances doesn't test how the app behaves under slow disks or network latency.
truths: Many failures are partial, not total.

analogy.title: Simulating a sprained ankle instead of removing a player
analogy.story: You learn how the team copes when someone is slowed down, not just absent.
analogy.breaks: Sprains heal slowly; FIS faults end exactly at the configured duration.

steps.label: Finding
steps.detail: Client timeouts too short; retries amplify load.

check.q: How does FIS inject CPU stress inside an EC2 instance?
check.a: By running an SSM document (e.g. AWSFIS-Run-CPU-Stress) via the aws:ssm:send-command action.

designing-safe-chaos-experiments-the-gam.core: Safe chaos follows a workflow: pick a critical scenario, write a steady-state hypothesis with SLIs, start small in staging, then limited production scope, define stop conditions and rollback, inform stakeholders, run as a game day with observers, document findings and fix them, then automate the experiment in CI/CD or on a schedule.

first_principles.problem: An ad-hoc chaos test in production causes a real outage and the programme gets cancelled.
derivation: **Scenario** from real risks (AZ loss, dependency latency).

analogy.title: Earthquake drills that increase in realism
analogy.story: Tabletop first, then a building drill, then a city-wide exercise.
analogy.breaks: Drills follow scripts; real systems may react unexpectedly, which is the point.

example.title: Quarterly game day
flow: Scenario: Aurora writer failover during peak
Run in staging, then 10% prod traffic window
Findings: connection pool doesn't refresh DNS → fix

check.q: Why start chaos experiments in staging?
check.a: To validate the experiment and safety controls before risking customer impact in production.
